Moon
MūN
n. (rendering Hebrew yārēach and lebānâh, and Greek selēnē)
From Old English mōna, common Germanic, from an Indo-European root meaning to measure — the same root that gives month, measure, and Latin mēnsis. The moon is named for its office: it is the great measurer, the clock hung in the sky. Hebrew has two words, yārēach (the ordinary name, tied to yerach, a month) and the poetic lebānâh, the white one. As with the sun, Genesis withholds the name on the fourth day and says only “the lesser light to rule the night” — a deliberate refusal to use the word the nations had made into a god.

Biblical Definition

The moon is the lesser light, made on the fourth day to rule the night and to serve, with the sun and stars, for signs and for seasons. Its borrowed brightness makes it the fitting emblem of derived and dependent glory: it rules, but it rules by reflection, having no light in itself. Israel's calendar hung on it, since the month began with the new moon and the feasts were reckoned from the months, so that the moon governed when the nation would assemble and worship. David makes it an argument for humility — “When I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars, which thou hast ordained; what is man, that thou art mindful of him?” (Psa 8:3-4) — where the vastness of the ordained lights magnifies the condescension of God toward a creature so small. The same ordained regularity becomes the ground of covenant assurance: the LORD gives the moon and stars for a light by night, and only if those ordinances depart shall the seed of Israel cease from being a nation. In the prophets the moon turned to blood is a sign of the great and terrible day of the LORD (Joe 2:31), quoted by Peter at Pentecost. Paul draws the last lesson: the glory of the moon differs from the glory of the sun and from the glory of the stars, and so it shall be in the resurrection (1Co 15:41) — glory is real, ordered, and unequal, and none of it is self-generated.

Webster 1828 Definition

The lesser light, made to rule the night and to measure the months; a creature shining by borrowed light, governing Israel's calendar of feasts, a witness to God's ordained constancy, and a sign in the prophets of the day of the LORD.

expand to see more

MOON, n. 1. The heavenly orb which revolves round the earth; a satellite of the earth. She rules the night by reflecting the light of the sun.

2. In Scripture, the lesser light appointed to rule the night, and with the sun and the stars to be for signs and for seasons. Genesis 1.

3. A month; the period of the moon's revolution. The word month is from moon, and in the Hebrew likewise, yerach a month from yareach the moon.

4. New moon; the beginning of the month, announced in Israel by the sound of trumpets and marked by appointed offerings. Numbers 10; Psalm 81.

5. The worship of the moon, as of the queen of heaven, was among the idolatries into which Israel fell, and was expressly rebuked by the prophet Jeremiah. Jer. 44.

Key Scripture

Psalm 8:3 — "When I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars, which thou hast ordained;"

Psalm 121:6 — "The sun shall not smite thee by day, nor the moon by night."

Joel 2:31 — "The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and the terrible day of the LORD come."

1 Corinthians 15:41 — "There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars: for one star differeth from another star in glory."

Modern Corruption

The moon was worshipped in the ancient world as the queen of heaven and is consulted in ours as a source of guidance and mood; both are the same refusal to let the lesser light be lesser.

expand to see more

Jeremiah records the plainest instance of the ancient error. The women of Judah in Egypt told the prophet outright that they would burn incense to the queen of heaven and pour out drink offerings to her, as their fathers had done, and that they had been better off when they did. Moon worship was not a fringe superstition but a household religion with a domestic economy attached, and God judged it. The law had already forbidden it by name, and Job disclaims it as a heart sin — if I beheld the moon walking in brightness, and my heart hath been secretly enticed, this were an iniquity to be punished by the judge.

The modern residue is astrology, in which the phases of the moon are read for temperament, fortune, and timing. It is worth naming plainly rather than smiling at, because Scripture treats it as a rival source of guidance, and Isaiah's mockery of the astrologers, the stargazers, the monthly prognosticators, is aimed exactly here. The Christian answer is not that the moon has no influence on tides and seasons, which it plainly has, but that it has no word. Guidance comes by Scripture and providence, from a God who speaks; the lights were given for signs and seasons, not for oracles.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yārēach is the ordinary name and is tied directly to yerach, a month; lebānâh is the poetic white one. Greek selēnē supplies the New Testament term, and the related verb gives the Gospels' word for those afflicted at the moon's changes.

expand to see more

Hebrew yārēach (H3394) — moon; some 27 occurrences, absent from Gen 1:16 where Moses says only “the lesser light.”

Hebrew lebānâh (H3842) — the moon as the white one, from lāban, to be white; the poetic term of Son 6:10 and Isa 24:23.

Hebrew chōdesh (H2320) — new moon, and thence the month; the day of the moon's renewal, kept with trumpets and offerings.

Greek selēnē (G4582) — moon; used in Act 2:20 of the moon turned into blood and in Rev 12:1 of the woman with the moon under her feet.

Greek selēniazomai (G4583) — to be moonstruck, rendered lunatick in Mat 4:24 and 17:15; the Authorized Version preserves the ancient association of the moon with these afflictions without endorsing it as their cause.

Usage

"Of the creature ruling the night: the lesser light (Gen 1:16); nor the moon by night (Psa 121:6); the moon and the stars which thou hast ordained (Psa 8:3)."

"Of the calendar of worship: the new moon and the sabbath (Isa 66:23; Col 2:16); blowing the trumpet in the new moon (Psa 81:3)."

"Of prophetic sign: the moon turned into blood (Joe 2:31; Act 2:20); the moon shall not give her light (Mat 24:29); the moon confounded when the LORD reigns in Zion (Isa 24:23)."
